summary: Calabasas occupies just 13.8 square miles of the Santa Monica Mountains' southern foothills, yet that footprint contains some of the most dramatic canyon-to-ridge topography in greater Los Angeles — the city's western edge borders Malibu Creek State Park, which means thousands of acres of publicly accessible sandstone gorges, oak woodlands, and chaparral ridgelines sit essentially at the municipal boundary. That proximity to serious open space is the headline, but the tradeoff is equally serious: a median home value near $1.45 million against a median household income of roughly $158,000 puts the price-to-income ratio above 9:1, meaning even a six-figure household faces steep math on a purchase. The city functions largely as a bedroom community for the entertainment and professional-services economy spread across the west San Fernando Valley and the Westside; the 101 freeway bisects the area and is both lifeline and bottleneck, with eastbound commutes toward Studio City or Century City reliably clogging during peak hours. Daily highs average 76°F with nearly ten hours of sunshine year-round, though summer afternoons in the inland canyons push well into the 90s — this is not coastal cool. Retail clusters along Calabasas Road and the Commons at Calabasas offer sit-down dining and upscale grocery options, but the overall commercial footprint is modest for a city of nearly 23,000, reinforcing the quiet-suburban pacing. The defining tension is spatial: world-class trail networks and golden-hour ridgeline views exist right alongside freeway noise and a housing cost structure that the local income median only barely services.
